title: Today in one sentence
text: On Thursday the S&P 500 fund SPY rose 0.3% and the Nasdaq 100 fund QQQ slipped 0.1%, so at the open watch whether chip stocks keep falling or bounce while drug and defense stocks stay strong; the next big test is next week, when GE, Meta and Lockheed report their results.

title: Drug and defense stocks held up while chips slid
text: On Thursday, Eli Lilly rose 3.5%, Lockheed Martin 2.0% and Intuitive Surgical 1.8%. In the same session Vertiv fell 3.6%, NVIDIA 1.8% and AMD 1.5%. When one group of stocks falls, money often moves to another group. Owning companies from different industries is called diversification, and days like this show why people like it.

title: Why Rocket Lab swings so much
text: Rocket Lab fell 6.6% on Thursday and sits near $55, far below its 52 week high of $151. Its beta is about 2.6, which means it has tended to move more than twice as much as the overall market. Big swings can go both ways, which is why our risk score for it is the highest on the list, 10 out of 10.

title: Three earnings reports start Tuesday
text: An earnings report is a company's report card for the last three months. GE Aerospace reports on Oct 20, Meta on Oct 21 and Lockheed Martin on Oct 22. Analysts expect earnings per share of about $2.01 for GE, $6.67 for Meta and $7.52 for Lockheed. Stocks often jump or drop on report days, even when the results are good.

title: Bond yields are the highest in a year
text: The 10 year Treasury yield is what the US government pays to borrow money for ten years. Its monthly average was 4.99% in September, up from 4.06% a year ago. Higher yields make safer bonds more attractive, and they can pull some money away from stocks.

title: Lesson 10: What is compound interest?
text: Compound interest means you earn growth on your growth. Say you invest $1,000 and it grows 7% in a year. You now have $1,070. Next year the 7% is applied to $1,070, not $1,000, so you gain $74.90 instead of $70. That small difference looks tiny at first, but it snowballs. At 7% a year, $1,000 becomes about $1,967 after 10 years and about $7,612 after 30 years. The most important ingredient is time, so starting early matters more than starting big. The 7% is only an example; real investments go up and down, and nothing is guaranteed.

title: What this covers
text: Prices are from Thursday's close. Analyst price targets and company numbers are available for NVIDIA, TSMC, AMD, Alphabet, Amazon, Microsoft, Meta, GE Aerospace and Lockheed Martin.
